field_guides.title: The cycle/post-cycle price signature
field_guides.dek: When the pipe is full, the price can look healthy all cycle and then sell off after the announcement. The two-sided game behind the print, why the calendar is the tell, and why the financial settlement captures the gaming while spot takes the unwind.

field_guides.title: Blending and equalization
field_guides.dek: Pipelines price quality on a scale frozen in 2014. The market prices it live. The gap between the two is the blender's business.

field_guides.title: How the CER regulates pipeline tolls
field_guides.dek: Pipeline tolls are the one part of the value chain a regulator actually prices. How they get negotiated, litigated, and trued up.

field_guides.title: Cokers: why WCS needs them
field_guides.dek: Delayed coking turns residue into light products and coke. The WCS discount to WTI is the market's price for that upgrade, and only complex refineries can collect it.

field_guides.title: Complexity, margins, and crude selection
field_guides.dek: Why hardware decides who can pay for which crude, why marginal yields set the bid, and why the industry keeps overbuilding conversion capacity.

field_guides.title: The 2021 Mainline contracting fight
field_guides.dek: In 2019 Enbridge tried to lock up 90 percent of the Mainline under long-term contracts. Producers revolted, and in November 2021 the CER said no: the pipe stays 100 percent uncommitted, which is why its apportionment numbers are the market's egress stress gauge.

field_guides.title: Diluent 101
field_guides.dek: The light oil that makes bitumen move, and the 30 percent of every dilbit barrel you are really buying.

field_guides.title: Where diluent comes from
field_guides.dek: Alberta produces about half the condensate it needs. The rest crosses the border from the United States, and the gap is widening.

field_guides.title: Drag-reducing agents and pipeline hydraulics
field_guides.dek: Chemistry is the cheapest pipeline capacity there is. A few parts per million of polymer can buy Trans Mountain 90,000 bpd, and the same physics explains why nameplate capacity is a reference point, not a physical constant.

field_guides.title: Egress 101
field_guides.dek: The pipes out of Alberta, apportionment, and why full pipes set the price.

field_guides.title: Force majeure and prorationing
field_guides.dek: When a pipeline breaks, the tariff decides who bleeds: what counts as force majeure, how the remaining capacity gets divided, and what three real outages did to differentials.

field_guides.title: Hardisty vs Edmonton
field_guides.dek: Canada prices its oil at two hubs, two hundred kilometres apart. Heavy at Hardisty, light and condensate at Edmonton, and a freight tariff in between.

field_guides.title: How a refinery actually works: the units
field_guides.dek: The process train in order: distillation, vacuum flashing, cracking, the octane shops, and the sulphur units, and what comes out the other end.

field_guides.title: How refineries actually buy crude
field_guides.dek: The monthly plan, the swap grid, and the barrels that move for no reason. How refinery crude buying really works, from the linear program (LP) run to the final bid.

field_guides.title: How upstream actually sells crude
field_guides.dek: The production plan, firm pipes, term deals, and the thin slice that sets the price. The sell side of the basin.

field_guides.title: How the Enbridge Mainline system works
field_guides.dek: The Mainline is the pipe system that carries roughly 70 percent of Western Canadian oil to market: about twenty lines run as one monthly nomination machine, with every barrel competing from zero each month because none of the capacity is contracted.

field_guides.title: Mine capacity vs upgrader capacity
field_guides.dek: Two plants, two numbers. Never blend them.

field_guides.title: Naphthenic (NFT) vs paraffinic (PFT) bitumen
field_guides.dek: Why some mined bitumen has to go through an upgrader, and some can go straight to a pipeline.

field_guides.title: Quality banks and assay differentials
field_guides.dek: Shared pipelines commingle everyone's crude. Quality banks settle the value differences, and the assay decides what your barrel is really worth.

field_guides.title: SAGD vs CSS vs mining
field_guides.dek: Steam-assisted gravity drainage (SAGD), cyclic steam stimulation (CSS), and mining: the three ways to get bitumen out of the ground.

field_guides.title: The synthetic grades
field_guides.dek: Synthetic Sweet Blend (SYN), Premium Albian, and the other light barrels of the oil sands.

field_guides.title: The Scotford chain
field_guides.dek: Muskeg River and Jackpine mines, the Corridor pipeline, and a Shell-operated upgrader outside Edmonton. How CNRL's mined bitumen becomes synthetic crude.

field_guides.title: How storage makes money: the carry
field_guides.dek: Buy the barrel now, sell it forward, put it in a tank. If the carry covers the full cost of holding it and both legs are truly matched, the profit is locked. Backwardation reverses the incentive.

field_guides.title: The Sturgeon refinery
field_guides.dek: The government-backed bitumen refinery northeast of Edmonton. Fifty thousand barrels a day of bitumen that never sees an export pipe.

field_guides.title: Trans Mountain: where it is and how it works
field_guides.dek: Canada's only pipeline to the Pacific coast: 890,000 barrels per day from Edmonton to Burnaby, a twinned system with its toll fight settled and more capacity coming.

field_guides.title: How turnarounds move barrels
field_guides.dek: Planned shutdowns, the Horizon September 2026 example, and why the calendar beats the snapshot.

field_guides.title: The upgrader interconnects
field_guides.dek: The bitumen lines between Suncor and Syncrude, and the unplanned-outage playbook they make possible.

field_guides.title: What is actually in Western Canadian Select
field_guides.dek: Western Canadian Select is a manufactured benchmark: about 20 Canadian heavy streams blended into one fungible barrel at Hardisty. The recipe is why refiners pay up or discount.

field_guides.title: How the WTI calendar month average works
field_guides.dek: The calendar month average (CMA) is the average of every daily West Texas Intermediate (WTI) settlement in a calendar month. It floats while the month trades, freezes when the month ends, and is implied from the futures strip before the month begins.

field_guides.title: Why this site uses z-scores
field_guides.dek: Raw volume moves mislead. The z-score measures each move against what is normal for that asset, so the unusual ones stand out.
